An element of a story I am creating is that Sylvanas tolerates the existence of a "cure" for being Forsaken; a potion created by the Tauren will re-animate Forsaken and give them life. In the stead of suppression of the potion (the leader of an entire faction certainly has the power to destroy all knowledge of a thing), she sees this potion as necessary for the continuance of the Forsaken.

A lorewise player with which I raised this very matter spoke of how the Forsaken are created post-LK versus pre-LK. They were tolerated before as they were the result of the LK's Plague of Undeath and were mostly human. (No participation on part of other Horde factions). Now they are raised from any corpse, including Horde, found by the Lesser Val'kyr who scour the world seeking suitable warriors.

There are factions, such as the Tauren, to whom the concept of being raised as an undead creature is anathema. They would rise up and likely destroy all those reanimated and deem it a kindness; their spirit is freed to rejoin Mother-Earth versus being trapped in a decaying body. The Orcs and Goblins would feel similarly but less opposed; the reanimated warriors can serve the purpose of combat, if nothing else. Likewise for the Blood Elves.

Sylvanas will be placed in the position of wanting the cure to exist and to suppress it; exerting her political power to secure the faction's future while this same exertion of her power would reduce Sylvanas in the eyes of the Horde. This is similar to Wotan in the Ring Cycle by Wagner. Wotan both desires the power of the Gods in Valhalla and also the Free Will of the Lesser Created Beings; humans and others. These contradictory forces are vital parts of the story.

This matter is addressed to the collective "Voat-mind". How speak thee?
